transcription.tex: Find the volume of a solid when a curve is revolved around either coordinate axis.
1. Rotate around the \(x\)-axis.\par Find the volume formed by rotating \(y=x^3\) about the \(x\)-axis between \(x=1\) and \(x=2\).
2. Rotate around the \(y\)-axis.\par Find the volume formed by rotating \(y=\sqrt{x+1}\) about the \(y\)-axis between \(y=1\) and \(y=2\).

3. Find more complex volumes by adding and subtracting.\par The area bounded by \(y=\sqrt{x}\) and \(y=x\) is rotated through \(360^\circ\) about the \(x\)-axis. Find the volume of the resulting solid.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: For \(f(x)\geq0\), \(\int_a^b y\,dx\) gives the area bounded by \(y=f(x)\), \(x=a\), \(x=b\) and the \(x\)-axis. Why?

Split the area into thin rectangular strips. Each has width \(dx\), height \(y=f(x)\), and area \(f(x)\,dx\).\par For discrete strips, add their areas: \(\sum f(x)\,\Delta x\).\par As the widths tend to zero, use \(\int\) instead of \(\Sigma\):\[A=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.\]Integration is a continuous version of summation.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: Spin \(y=f(x)\) about the \(x\)-axis to form a solid of revolution. How can we use the same principle as before? What replaces strips?
Rotate the curve around the axis.
Use infinitely thin cylinders, each with width \(dx\) and radius \(y\).
Each thin cylinder has volume:
Add all the thin cylinders:
\[V=\pi\int_a^b y^2\,dx.\]Square the function and put a factor of \(\pi\) in front.

transcription.tex: [Textbook] The diagram shows the region \(R\) which is bounded by the \(x\)-axis, the \(y\)-axis and the curve with equation \(y=9-{x}^{2}\). The region is rotated through \(360^{\circ}\) about the \(x\)-axis. Find the exact volume of the solid generated.

Find the roots first:\[9-x^2=0\implies x=\pm3.\]Use the positive region:\[V=\pi\int_0^3(9-x^2)^2\,dx\]\[=\pi\int_0^3(81-18x^2+x^4)\,dx\]\[=\pi\left[81x-6x^3+\tfrac15x^5\right]_0^3\]\[=\pi\left(\tfrac{648}5-0\right)=\tfrac{648\pi}5.\]

transcription.tex: 8. \(y=x\sqrt{4-x^2}\). Region \(R\) lies between the curve, the \(x\)-axis and \(x=a\), where \(0<a<2\), as shown. Rotation through \(2\pi\) radians about the \(x\)-axis gives volume \(657\pi/160\). Find \(a\).

\[V=\pi\int_a^2(x\sqrt{4-x^2})^2\,dx\]\[=\pi\int_a^2x^2(4-x^2)\,dx\]\[=\pi\int_a^2(4x^2-x^4)\,dx\]\[=\pi[4x^3/3-x^5/5]_a^2\]\[=\pi\bigl((32/3-32/5)-(4a^3/3-a^5/5)\bigr)\]\[=\frac\pi{15}(64-20a^3+3a^5).\]\[V=657\pi/160\implies3a^5-20a^3+77/32=0.\]Try \(a=1\): \(-467/32\ne0\). Try \(a=1/2\): the expression is zero. Thus \(a-1/2\) is a factor and \(a=1/2\). The volume strictly decreases on \(0<a<2\), so this is the unique solution.

slides.title: Prove the Volume of a Sphere

transcription.tex: Prove that the volume of a sphere is \(V=\tfrac43\pi r^3\).

For the circle,\[x^2+y^2=r^2,\quad y=\pm\sqrt{r^2-x^2}.\]Rotate the upper semicircle about the \(x\)-axis. First find one hemisphere:\[V_{\mathrm{half}}=\pi\int_0^r(\sqrt{r^2-x^2})^2\,dx\]\[=\pi\int_0^r(r^2-x^2)\,dx\]\[=\pi[r^2x-x^3/3]_0^r\]\[=\pi((r^3-r^3/3)-0)=\tfrac23\pi r^3.\]Double this:\[V=2\left(\tfrac23\pi r^3\right)=\tfrac43\pi r^3.\]

transcription.tex: 9. Right-angled triangle \(R\) has width \(r\) and height \(h\). Rotate it through \(2\pi\) radians about the \(y\)-axis. Use integration to show the cone has volume \(V=\tfrac13\pi r^2h\).

The hypotenuse has gradient \(h/r\), so\[y=\frac hr x\implies x^2=\frac{r^2}{h^2}y^2.\]\[V=\pi\int_0^h\frac{r^2}{h^2}y^2\,dy\]\[=\frac{\pi r^2}{h^2}[y^3/3]_0^h\]\[=\frac{\pi r^2}{h^2}(h^3/3-0)\]\[=\tfrac13\pi r^2h.\]

transcription.tex: The region \(R\) is bounded by \(y=x^3+2\), \(y=5-2x\) and the coordinate axes. (a) Verify that the intersection \(A\) is \((1,3)\). (b) Rotate \(R\) through \(360^\circ\) about the \(x\)-axis; find the volume.
\[1^3+2=3,\qquad5-2(1)=3.\]Both equations pass through \((1,3)\).

Find the two volumes separately.\[V_1=\pi\int_0^1(x^3+2)^2\,dx=36\pi/7.\]\(5-2x\) meets the axis at \(x=2.5\). The second solid is a cone of radius 3 and height 1.5:\[V_2=\tfrac13\pi(3^2)(1.5)=9\pi/2.\]\[V=36\pi/7+9\pi/2=135\pi/14.\]

transcription.tex: Region \(R\) is bounded by \(y=\sqrt x\), \(y=1/(8x)\) and \(x=1\). Rotate \(R\) through \(360^\circ\) about the \(x\)-axis. Find the exact volume.

Find the volume under the top curve and subtract the volume under the bottom curve.\par Intersection:\[\frac1{8x}=\sqrt x\implies8x^{3/2}=1\implies x=\tfrac14.\]\[V_1=\pi\int_{1/4}^1(\sqrt x)^2\,dx=15\pi/32.\]\[V_2=\pi\int_{1/4}^1(1/(8x))^2\,dx=3\pi/64.\]\[V_R=15\pi/32-3\pi/64=27\pi/64.\]

transcription.tex: The area between \(y=x\) and \(y=\sqrt[3]x\), where \(x\geq0\), is rotated through \(360^\circ\) about the \(x\)-axis. Find the volume.

\[x=x^{1/3}\implies x^3=x\implies x^3-x=0.\]\[x(x-1)(x+1)=0\implies x=-1,0,1.\]Use \(0\leq x\leq1\).\[V_1=\pi\int_0^1(x^{1/3})^2\,dx=3\pi/5.\]The inner solid is a cone:\[V_2=\tfrac13\pi(1^2)(1)=\pi/3.\]\[V_R=3\pi/5-\pi/3=4\pi/15.\]

transcription.tex: 4. The shape is bounded by \(y=\tfrac12x^2\), \(2x+y=6\) and \(2x-y=-6\). (a) Find \(A\) and \(B\). (b) Rotate the shape about the \(y\)-axis; find the volume.

transcription.tex: 4. An egg timer is 16 cm high and modelled as a solid of revolution about the \(y\)-axis. Its upper curve is \(x=\sqrt[3]y\), with a matching lower half. Sand flows at 8 cm³/min. The timer must empty in 5 minutes. Find, to 2 decimal places, the initial height of sand in the top half.

The sand volume is \(8\times5=40\ \mathrm{cm}^3\). Let \(b\) be its height.\[40=\pi\int_0^b(\sqrt[3]y)^2\,dy\]\[40=\pi[3y^{5/3}/5]_0^b\]\[40=\tfrac35\pi b^{5/3}\]\[b^{5/3}=\frac{200}{3\pi}\]\[b=\left(\frac{200}{3\pi}\right)^{3/5}=6.25\ \mathrm{cm}.\]
